source.title: Theoretical descriptions of compound-nuclear reactions: open problems & challenges

accepted.question_text: How can compound-nuclear reaction theory be extended to reactions on light nuclei and on nuclei away from the valley of stability when the density of compound-nucleus resonances is too small for a purely statistical treatment, but the number of resonances is still too large to permit an individual resonance-by-resonance treatment?

evidence.quote: It has long been known that these conditions are not always fulfilled, e.g. for reactions on light nuclei, when the density of CN resonances becomes too small for a statistical treatment, but the number of resonances remains too large to allow for an individual treatment [52].
Similar difficulties can be expected for the application of reaction theories to nuclei away from the valley of stability.

accepted.question_text: How can direct-reaction and compound-nucleus components be described within a single coherent framework so that their respective contributions can be disentangled in reactions involving rare isotopes and in indirect cross-section extraction problems?

evidence.quote: To disentangle the components, it becomes important to describe them in a coherent framework.

Understanding the interplay of direct and compound reaction mechanisms becomes very important for extracting cross sections indirectly from surrogate measurements, as well as for interpreting experiments with rare isotopes.

accepted.question_text: What practical approximation methods can reproduce the weak-absorption compound-nucleus cross sections and width-fluctuation effects that are treated by the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble reference approach, while avoiding the computational cost of the full closed-form calculation and improving approximate expressions for the width-fluctuation correction factor Wcc′?

evidence.quote: However, it requires a computationally expensive calculation of a triple integral that enters the closed-form expression for the average cross section [76].
While the GOE approach is often considered a reference to which other theories should be compared, approximate methods are needed for practical applications.
In recent years, there has been renewed focus on testing various approximate expressions for Wcc′ against the GOE approach [51] and to develop improvements [56].

accepted.question_text: What additional physics is required in preequilibrium reaction models to achieve a general description of preequilibrium reactions in regimes where equilibrium is not reached and a statistical compound-nucleus description is therefore inapplicable?

evidence.quote: At the same time, a statistical compound nucleus type of description cannot be used either, as equilibrium is not reached.
We concluded there that the existing preequilibrium models still fall far short of including the physics necessary for a general description of these reactions.

accepted.question_text: How can the compound-nucleus formation process in a surrogate reaction be modeled accurately enough that cross sections extracted indirectly from surrogate measurements are reliable?

evidence.quote: The accuracy of the extracted cross section depends on how well the compound-nucleus formation process in the surrogate reaction is described.

accepted.question_text: How can low-energy radioactive-beam experiments separate compound-reaction contributions from direct-reaction contributions well enough to yield reliable nuclear-structure information?

evidence.quote: Similarly, separating the compound and direct-reaction contributions in low-energy radioactive beam experiments is crucial for obtaining reliable nuclear structure information.

accepted.question_text: Which theoretical developments missing from widely used Hauser-Feshbach-based reaction codes, and which underlying assumptions of those descriptions, must be implemented or tested in order to obtain reliable and comprehensive descriptions of compound-nuclear reactions?

evidence.quote: Despite the wide use of the Hauser-Feshbach formalism in modern reaction codes, some of the available theoretical developments have not yet been implemented and some of the underlying assumptions remain to be tested.

We find that various questions and challenges remain to be addressed in order to gain a deeper understanding of the many-body processes involved and to obtain reliable, comprehensive descriptions of this important class of nuclear reactions.
